extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (especially academics and prospective authors) considering writing a mathematics book
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and editorial guidance for planning, writing, revising, indexing, and submitting a mathematics book aimed at graduate/advanced audiences; addresses technical production (LaTeX), workflow, and interaction with publishers and reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have something original to say
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are only repeating, or paraphrasing, what has been said before then you are contributing nothing to the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A book must contribute new viewpoint or material; do not write merely to restate existing expositions. If you have nothing new to say, do not embark on the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a detailed plan / outline / TOC
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by writing chapter headings, then section headings; write a detailed outline of the book and carry it with you mentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the TOC as detailed as possible; treat it like essential exercise—if you cannot write a TOC you may not have a book. The TOC need not be immutable; it can evolve, but having the entire vision helps keep perspective and prevent detours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay writing a book until established (tenure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not consider writing a book until you have tenure and are established somewhere: the task is too time consuming and often not viewed positively in tenure decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assistant professors are advised to focus on papers and establishing research reputation first; once tenured you will have the leisure for a book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immerse yourself in the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoroughly immerse yourself—the book becomes your 'world' for a couple of years; jot down thoughts or topics as they occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constant involvement produces ideas in lectures, conversations, or daydreams; keep notes (notebook or computer file) to capture stray insights for later chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write one chapter at a time and stay focused
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a chapter at a time and completely immerse yourself in each chapter; if thoughts about other chapters occur, note them for later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although computers let you jump between chapters, that can be confusing; safest practice is to make a note of cross-chapter thoughts and return to them when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt the reader's perspective (reverse evolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Put yourself in the shoes of the learner (e.g., first-year graduate student) and anticipate where they will get hung up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exercise helps you see motivation and foundations and identify obscurities; design exposition to help the novice progress through the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize so lemmas and definitions appear before use
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend to details: ensure all lemmas and definitions are in place where needed; avoid parenthetical, belated proofs or definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: inserting a lemma parenthetically (e.g., ‘‘Proof: Let ... Calculate ...’’) is a 'love letter to yourself' that confuses readers. Use explicit placement and connecting material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough line-by-line revision and willingness to rewrite
rubrics_metrics.description: To turn drafts into a publishable book you must go through the manuscript line by line, attending to context, syntax, logic, motivation, and often rewrite whole sections or chapters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revision is tedious and may require discarding drafts; 'only wimps revise their manuscripts; great authors throw their work in the trash and rewrite'—use common sense and selective application, but expect multiple passes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom-test the material by teaching first
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop course lecture notes, teach the subject several times, polish notes, and use student/colleague feedback as a take-off point for the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: live testing of exposition, natural development and revision, safe environment for feedback, and an opportunity to abandon without losing face if the material doesn't develop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider a collaborator but be aware of downsides
rubrics_metrics.description: A collaborator can provide reality checks, enthusiasm, and shared work—but collaboration introduces scheduling, personal, and coordination risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaboration is like adding family; it can become dysfunctional. Weigh benefits (motivation, sanity check) against potential conflicts or divergent life circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have the entire vision before launching full writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to have the entire vision of the book in place before you launch full steam into writing to keep perspective and avoid wandering into detours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planned approach is generally superior, though sometimes allowing the project to evolve can work; planning helps know what remains to be done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write and polish the Preface carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: The Preface is paramount: it is part of planning and acts as a touchstone; it explains why existing books don't fill the need, the right level, prerequisites, and point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers and readers study the Preface and TOC; use it to deflect readers' 'Buts' and to organize your aims. Even if later it changes, writing it is a valuable organizing exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Table of Contents as a planning and organizing tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The TOC previews the book's milestones and big ideas; writing it helps launch Chapter 1 and clarifies the project's feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing the TOC feels impossible, reconsider the project. Use LaTeX (	ableofcontents) to produce TOC automatically; be detailed but flexible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a concept-based, thorough index (author should make it)
rubrics_metrics.description: Index by concept, not by word, so readers can find topics quickly; a thorough index greatly increases a book's usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern tools (LaTeX \\index, \\makeindex, makeindex) simplify the job; although professional indexers exist, the author knows the book best and should create the index. Tag entries as you write to ease later compilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appendices to avoid interrupting exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Place painful calculations, technical lemmas, background results, or alternative approaches in appendices to keep the main text flowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State in the text that details are relegated to an appendix to preserve exposition; appendices are an effective device to manage technical material and author psyche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare bibliography, table of notation, and glossary
rubrics_metrics.description: A good bibliography, detailed index, table of notation, and optional glossary increase the book's value and accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tasks are tedious but important; LaTeX macros and existing references can assist (see referenced sections/books). Their presence can broaden the book's audience beyond specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan time management: balance long-range planning with narrow focus
rubrics_metrics.description: You must plan the entire project to avoid hidden problems but adopt a narrow, section-level focus when actually writing to make incremental progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'living one day at a time' shortsightedness; pick a section and finish it, note other worries for later. Bouncing around is a path to failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt and be aware of a workflow method (spiral vs organic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Halmos's spiral method: write Chapter 1, then 2, then rewrite earlier chapters iteratively; organic (computer) approach allows simultaneous edits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spiral gives discrete control but may over-attend early chapters; organic editing can lead to a vortex of changes. Choose what works and be mindful of side effects (e.g., book may get looser later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for writer's block and have strategies to persist
rubrics_metrics.description: Many books stall partway; writer's block or difficult expositions can prevent completion unless countered by planning, incremental progress, and stamina.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that difficulties are normal (as in research); plan where difficulties may lie and address them systematically; incremental programs reduce risk of abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission strategy: multiple simultaneous submissions are acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike journal papers, you may submit a book manuscript simultaneously to several publishers; provide prospectus/TOC/sample chapters to jump-start negotiations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarize yourself with publishers' lists and series; send Prospectus, TOC, sample chapters, and a cover letter. Early submittals can be used to seek typing grants or advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide publishers with essential metadata about the book
rubrics_metrics.description: Be ready to supply subject matter and working title; level (graduate/undergraduate/professional); classes the book could serve; competing texts; working length; and expected date of completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers need this for marketing, scheduling and pricing. Erratic changes from contracted estimates (length, subject, schedule) can harm relations with the publisher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send materials in a manner that gets publisher attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit manuscripts via registered/certified/express mail to ensure special treatment, or as PDF attachments by email with detailed description of remitted materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical special mail often receives priority; in modern practice email PDF attachments are acceptable—explain exactly what you are sending, suggest reviewers, and attach CV. Keep records (return receipt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat reviewer reports as constructive feedback; you remain responsible
rubrics_metrics.description: Read reviews intensely and dispassionately to learn how the manuscript reads to others; do not react emotionally. Reviewers are not responsible for correctness—ultimate responsibility lies with the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect 2–4 reviews over a few months; use reviewer comments to improve the manuscript in the post-review period (last chance for substantial rewriting). Do not assume reviewer pass implies correctness—check every word yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow publishers' formatting and page-proof workflows
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers often want double or triple spaced manuscripts to allow copy editors and typesetters room for markings; modern workflows are electronic with PDF proofs and electronic sticky notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use LaTeX commands (e.g., \openup) to adjust spacing if needed. Be prepared for page proofs stage where final indexing and proofreading occur; this is when the final index is often assembled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use LaTeX indexing workflow (\index, \makeindex, makeindex)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tag index entries in the source using \index{...}, include \makeindex after \begin{document}, compile to produce .idx, process with makeindex to create .ind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing by tagging as you write avoids the old card-based workflow; makeindex alphabetizes and removes redundancies; the process typically takes only a few hours and software/macros can assist.
